issue.title: bats exits zero when first argument is empty string
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**
When invoked with an empty first parameter (instead of a file or directory that exists), bats collects 0 tests and exits 0.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. invoke `bats ""`

**Expected behavior**
Exit 1 (or otherwise nonzero) as it would if the first argument were a file path or directory that did not exist.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - Bats version: 1.12.0
 - operating system (including version): macOS 15.5
 - `bash --version`: `GNU bash, version 5.3.3(1)-release (aarch64-apple-darwin24.6.0)`
 - Install method: nixpkgs

**Additional context**
The invocation is, of course, nonsensical. But we ran into this in nixpkgs testing when a change caused something like `bats "$varName"` to start expanding to `bats ""`, and we didn't notice since the tests were still passing.

issue.title: Formatter "pretty" is not the default anymore in version 1.14.0
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

From the `--help` output: `  -F, --formatter <type>    Switch between formatters: pretty (default),`

I noticed that when I run a bats test file in version 1.14.0 (`bats my-tests.bats`), that the output is not formatted _pretty_ anymore.

To workaround, the pretty formatter must be explicitly set: `bats --pretty my-tests.bats`

Switching back to 1.13.0 fixes the issue. I think https://github.com/bats-core/bats-core/pull/1191 introduced this regression.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - Bats version 1.14.0
 - Debian 12
 - `bash --version`: GNU bash, version 5.2.15(1)-release
 - Install method: git

issue.title: --allow-empty-suite forces a hard dependency on bats >= 1.14
issue.body:
### Describe the bug

Since v1.14.0 (PR #1211) an empty test suite results in an error, which is incompatible with older bats versions. It breaks some existing setups (see below for an example). The suggested workaround is to add `--allow-empty-suite` to get the old behavior back.

Unfortunately, the workaround itself is also incompatible with older bats versions, as any old version will error out with `Bad command line option '--allow-empty-suite'`.

So for a project that legitimately produces an empty suite in some configuration, the choice is:

* add `--allow-empty-suite` and drop support for every bats before 1.14, or
* pin bats to <= 1.13 and stay on an old version.

### To Reproduce

Real-world example, https://github.com/containers/conmon/pull/672: CRI-O's test runner always makes two bats passes, the second one selecting the serial tests:

```
execute bats --jobs "$JOBS" --tap "${TESTS[@]}" --filter-tags '!crio:serial'
execute bats --tap "${TESTS[@]}" --filter-tags 'crio:serial'
```

When the requested test set contains no serial test, the second pass legitimately has nothing to run, and with v1.14.0 CI fails:

```
+ bats --tap critest.bats --filter-tags crio:serial
1..0
ERROR: Found no tests. (Try `--allow-empty-suite`?)
```

Adding `--allow-empty-suite` there would have broken the distro-provided older bats that other jobs use, so we had to pin bats to v1.13.0 instead.

### Expected behavior

A way to opt into the old behavior that older bats versions silently ignore, i.e. an environment variable — `BATS_ALLOW_EMPTY_SUITE=1` — with the same effect as `--allow-empty-suite`. Older versions ignore an unknown `BATS_*` variable and keep exiting 0 on an empty suite, which is exactly the behavior being asked for, so one setting works across versions.

There is precedent for flags having an environment variable equivalent, e.g. `--code-quote-style` / `$BATS_CODE_QUOTE_STYLE`.

### Environment

* bats 1.14.0

issue.title: `bats_test_function` false "Duplicate test name(s)" when one dynamic test's args are a prefix of another's
issue.body:
**Component:** `libexec/bats-core/bats-gather-tests`
**Version:** bats-core 1.13.0 (also present at `d9faff0`, i.e. `v1.13.0-33-gd9faff0`)
**Affected function:** `bats_test_function` (dedup check added at gather time)

## Summary

When a test file registers dynamically-parametrized tests via `bats_test_function`
(the pattern used for data-driven tests, e.g. one function run with different
argument tuples), bats aborts the whole file with a false
`ERROR: Duplicate test name(s) in file "...": <name>` whenever one registered
call's `function name + args` string happens to be a literal **prefix** of another
call's string for the *same* function. This is a false positive: the two calls have
different arguments and are not duplicates. Whether the bug triggers depends on the
**registration order** of the two calls within the file, which for callers building
the argument list from an associative array (e.g. iterating `"${!some_assoc_array[@]}"`
to call `bats_test_function` in a loop) is effectively bash hash-order-dependent and
not under the test author's control.

## Root cause

In `bats_test_function` (`libexec/bats-core/bats-gather-tests`):

```bash
line="$BATS_TEST_FILENAME"
line+=$'\t'
line+="$*"
...
# dereferencing ${test_names[*]} fails on older bash versions when empty -> check before
if [[ ${#test_names[@]} -gt 0 && " ${test_names[*]} " == *" $line "* ]]; then
    test_dupes+=("$line")
fi
test_names+=("$line")
```

Each test's identity is `<filename>\t<function-name-and-args>`. Duplicate detection
joins all previously-seen identities with spaces and does a **substring** glob
match (`*" $line "*`) instead of an exact per-element comparison. Because `IFS`
(space) also appears *inside* `$*` whenever a call has multiple arguments, a
shorter identity string can end up embedded, padded by spaces, inside a longer one
— even though the two are genuinely different `line` values with different
`$*` args.

Concretely: registering `f --format plain` and then `f` (bare, no args) produces
these two `line` values (tab-separated filename omitted for brevity):

- `f --format plain`
- `f`

Joining as `" f --format plain f "` and searching for `*" f "*` matches, because
`f ` appears right before `--format` — the search string `" f "` is a substring of
`" f --format plain f "` purely by coincidence of word boundaries, not because `f`
(no args) was ever actually registered before.

## Reproduction

```bash
# prefix.bats — longer args registered FIRST, shorter (bare) SECOND
f() { :; }
bats_test_function --description "long one" -- f --format plain
bats_test_function --description "short one" -- f
```

```
$ bats prefix.bats
ERROR: Duplicate test name(s) in file "prefix.bats": f
```

Swapping the registration order makes the false positive disappear, confirming the
substring/order dependency and that this is not a real duplicate:

```bash
# prefix-reversed.bats — same two calls, shorter (bare) registered FIRST
f() { :; }
bats_test_function --description "short one" -- f
bats_test_function --description "long one" -- f --format plain
```

```
$ bats prefix-reversed.bats
1..2
ok 1 short one
ok 2 long one
```

Both files declare the exact same two logical tests; only the registration order
differs, and only one order is (falsely) rejected.

## Impact

Any file that dynamically parametrizes tests over a set of CLI-flag-shaped argument
strings — e.g. building test cases from an associative array and calling
`bats_test_function` in a `for description in "${!cases[@]}"` loop — can hit this
whenever one case's argument string happens to be a prefix of another's for the same
underlying function (a very natural situation: a "default"/bare case next to a case
that adds one more flag on top). Because the loop iterates over hash-table keys,
whether the bug fires can flip between runs/bash versions with no change to the test
file itself, making it read as flaky/nondeterministic when it is really a
registration-order artifact of a substring-match dedup check.

## Related: bats-core#1036

[bats-core#1036](https://github.com/bats-core/bats-core/issues/1036) (open,
confirmed) reports that gathering empty tests scales ~O(n²) with test count (0.24s
at 1 test, 242s at 1000). That's this same dedup check: on every
`bats_test_function` call it rebuilds `" ${test_names[*]} "` (already O(n) in the
tests seen so far) and glob-scans it, so the file-level cost is O(n²) even before
considering correctness. #1036's repro uses unique per-test titles, so it isn't
hitting the prefix false-positive described here — it's the same root design (an
ever-growing collection re-scanned from scratch on every call) surfacing as a
performance bug instead of a correctness one. Worth linking the two when filing.

## Suggested fix

Compare identities exactly instead of via substring/glob match. An associative
array would be the obvious tool, but this file explicitly supports Bash 3 (see the
"avoid unbound variable with set -u Bash 3" comments a few lines above the bug, at
lines 71 and 88) and `declare -A` is Bash-4+ only, so the fix needs to stay
Bash-3-compatible.

**Minimal fix (correctness only):** a plain exact-match scan over the existing
array, no new data structure:

```bash
local is_dupe=false existing
for existing in "${test_names[@]}"; do
    if [[ "$existing" == "$line" ]]; then
        is_dupe=true
        break
    fi
done
"$is_dupe" && test_dupes+=("$line")
test_names+=("$line")
```

This preserves the existing behaviour for genuine duplicates (identical filename +
function + args registered twice) while eliminating false positives from prefix
relationships between distinct argument strings, and removes the order-dependence —
all without raising the Bash version floor. It's still O(n²) per file overall
(one O(n) scan per call), so on its own it does **not** fix #1036 — merely stops it
from also being wrong.

**Fix that also addresses #1036:** move duplicate detection out of the per-call hot
path entirely. Keep `test_names+=("$line")` as the only per-call work, then once at
the end of gathering (e.g. in `bats_gather_tests`, after the file has been fully
sourced), sort the collected array once and scan for adjacent equal entries:

```bash
local sorted_names
IFS=$'\n' sorted_names=($(sort <<<"${test_names[*]}")) # or `sort -z` with a NUL-joined build if names may contain newlines
unset IFS
local i
for ((i = 1; i < ${#sorted_names[@]}; i++)); do
    [[ "${sorted_names[i]}" == "${sorted_names[i-1]}" ]] && test_dupes+=("${sorted_names[i]}")
done
```

This is O(n log n) per file (dominated by `sort`), fixes the same false-positive
(exact-value comparison, no substring search) and directly addresses #1036's
complaint, at the cost of a slightly larger change (duplicate detection moves from
"as you register" to "after the file is fully gathered").

issue.title: Make -- a valid command line option and follow the convention of it being the terminator for all options
issue.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

This relates to #863. I encountered it when working around the issue of dotfiles not being shown by setting `GLOBIGNORE=".:.."`, then invoking `bats *.bats`.

ShellCheck rightly pointed out that confusion could occur between command line options and files starting with `--` when using a bare glob.

The convention in most GNU utils these days is to allow `--` and assume that this terminates the list of options. Everything past that point is treated as a list of files/directories/items ...

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I would propose to allow for `--` and have it signal the end of the list of options.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Currently I am simply using `./*.bats`, which also dodges the issue.

issue.title: confusing use of color when tests not executed
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**
This issue concerns tests that specifically are not _executed_ -- it does not concern tests that are _skipped_.

When all tests run and pass or are skipped, a green color is used in the summary output. When any tests fail, a red color is used in the summary output. When one or more tests are not executed and the rest pass or are skipped, the green color is still used -- this is confusing, as a test not executing indicates an aberrant condition, IMO. The color should be the one used for failure, or perhaps a third, warning color (e.g. yellow)

**To Reproduce**
1. create a simple test case with two tests, one that passes and one that is not executed
2. execute the test case

I don't know if there's a normal way for a test to not be executed (as opposed to skipped). I encountered this via [this bug](https://github.com/bats-core/bats-file/issues/40).

**Expected behavior**
When one or more tests are not executed and the rest of the tests pass or are skipped, the summary color should be the one used for failure, or perhaps a third, warning color (e.g. yellow).

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - Bats Version: da56a30
 - OS: MacOS 11.6.1
 - Bash version: 5.1.12(1) (from MacPorts)

**Additional context**
![Screen Shot 2022-01-14 at 9 35 34 AM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2432691/149533173-8a1160dc-d84b-4323-8a8f-452e21ea918e.png)

issue.title: Tests with non-ASCII names are silently never executed under a UTF-8 locale (locale-dependent [[:alnum:]] in bats_encode_test_name)
issue.body:
## Summary

`bats_encode_test_name` in `libexec/bats-core/bats-preprocess` decides between two
encoding strategies with a **locale-dependent** regex:

```sh
if [[ ! "$name" =~ [^[:alnum:]\ _-] ]]; then
```

Under `LC_ALL=C` this is false for any non-ASCII name, so the safe hex-encoding branch
runs and the generated function name is pure ASCII.

Under a UTF-8 locale, `[[:alnum:]]` matches CJK, Cyrillic, Hangul, fullwidth and accented
letters. The condition becomes **true**, the "fast" branch runs, and the raw multibyte
bytes are embedded directly into the generated shell function name.

For a subset of those names, `declare -F` in `bats_perform_test`
(`libexec/bats-core/bats-exec-test:320`) then fails to find the function, and the test
**never runs** — while the TAP plan line still counts it.

## Impact

The `1..N` plan line reports the declared count. The tests that ghosted produce no
`ok`/`not ok` line at all. On a suite where this went unnoticed, we measured
**889 declared / 804 executed — 85 tests that had not run for an unknown length of time.**

bats does print `# bats warning: Executed N instead of expected M tests` and exits
non-zero, so this is not *fully* silent. But the diagnostic is easy to lose in practice:
it goes to stderr as a comment line, and any pipeline that ends in `| tail`, a formatter,
or a CI step that only inspects the last lines will show a plan of N and a screen of
`ok` lines. The tests are gone, and the report looks healthy.

This is a false-green failure mode in a test runner, which is why we are filing it even
though a warning exists.

## Reproduction

```sh
cat > t.bats <<'EOF'
@test "pure ascii" { true; }
@test "あ" { true; }
@test "中" { true; }
@test "件" { true; }
@test "Кириллица" { true; }
@test "한국어" { true; }
@test "café" { true; }
@test "Ａ" { true; }
EOF

LC_ALL=C           bats t.bats; echo "rc=$?"
LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 bats t.bats; echo "rc=$?"
```

### Actual

```
$ LC_ALL=C bats t.bats
1..8
ok 1 pure ascii
ok 2 あ
ok 3 中
ok 4 件
ok 5 Кириллица
ok 6 한국어
ok 7 café
ok 8 Ａ
rc=0

$ LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 bats t.bats
1..8
ok 1 pure ascii
bats: unknown test name `$'test_\343\201\202''
bats: unknown test name `$'test_\344\270\255''
ok 4 件
bats: unknown test name `$'test_\320\232\320\270...''
bats: unknown test name `$'test_\355\225\234...''
ok 7 café
ok 8 Ａ
# bats warning: Executed 4 instead of expected 8 tests
rc=1
```

Same binary, same file, same bash. Only `LC_ALL` differs.

## Confirming the branch flip directly

Extracting `bats_encode_test_name` verbatim and calling it on the same inputs:

| input | `LC_ALL=C` | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8` |
|---|---|---|
| `あ` | slow path → `test_-ffff…e3-ffff…81-ffff…82` | **fast path → `test_あ`** |
| `件` | slow path → `test_-ffff…e4-ffff…bb-ffff…b6` | **fast path → `test_件`** |
| `café` | slow path (ASCII-safe) | **fast path → `test_café`** |

So the locale controls which branch is taken. That part is fully determined.

## What we could NOT determine (open question for maintainers)

Under a UTF-8 locale **every** one of the names above takes the fast path and gets a raw
multibyte function name — yet only some of them fail to dispatch:

| name | codepoint | UTF-8 | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `件` | U+4EF6 | `E4 BB B6` | **runs** |
| `中` | U+4E2D | `E4 B8 AD` | ghosts |
| `亜` | U+4E9C | `E4 BA 9C` | ghosts |
| `あ` | U+3042 | `E3 81 82` | ghosts |
| `ア` | U+30A2 | `E3 82 A2` | ghosts |
| `К` | U+041A | `D0 9A` | ghosts |
| `한` | U+D55C | `ED 95 9C` | ghosts |
| `é` | U+00E9 | `C3 A9` | **runs** |
| `Ａ` | U+FF21 | `EF BC A1` | **runs** |

`件` and `中` are both CJK ideographs in the same block and differ only in codepoint, so
**the boundary is per-codepoint, not per-script and not per-length.** We tested and ruled
out: number of multibyte characters, script/block, and mixing with ASCII.

Separately, bash itself has no problem with these names — defining and calling
`test_あ`, `test_中`, `test_한` etc. directly all succeed in the same shell. So the loss
happens somewhere between the preprocessor emitting the definition and
`declare -F "${BATS_TEST_NAME%% *}"` resolving it, and we did not isolate where.

We are reporting the boundary as **uncharacterized** rather than guessing.

## Why the fix does not depend on that open question

Regardless of which raw-multibyte names happen to survive, the fast path exists as an
optimisation for names that are *already* safe as shell identifiers. Non-ASCII names are
not. Making the guard locale-independent restores the hex-encoding path for every
non-ASCII name and removes the whole class:

```diff
-  if [[ ! "$name" =~ [^[:alnum:]\ _-] ]]; then
+  if [[ ! "$name" =~ [^a-zA-Z0-9\ _-] ]]; then
```

An explicit ASCII class is preferable to wrapping the comparison in `LC_ALL=C`, because
it states the intent (shell-identifier-safe) rather than depending on ambient locale.

The same locale sensitivity applies to the `[[ "$char" =~ [[:alnum:]] ]]` test on line 22
inside the slow path, which should get the same treatment for consistency.

## Environment

- bats-core **1.13.0** (Homebrew), macOS 26.x, arm64, `bash` 3.2.57
- Also reproduced on **bats-core 1.14.0** on a second macOS machine
  (21-case matrix: `declared=21 / executed=16 / 5 ghosts / rc=1` under `en_US.UTF-8`;
  `declared=21 / executed=21 / 0 ghosts / rc=0` under `LC_ALL=C`)

The version is not the variable — the locale is. A machine whose ambient environment has
`LC_ALL`/`LC_CTYPE`/`LANG` unset behaves like `LC_ALL=C` and will not show the bug, which
makes it easy for this to reproduce on one developer's machine and not another's.

## Detection for existing suites

For anyone who wants to check whether their suite is already affected, comparing the
declared count against the executed count per file is sufficient:

```sh
bats tests/ > out.tap 2>&1
declared=$(/usr/bin/grep -oE '^1\.\.[0-9]+' out.tap | /usr/bin/grep -oE '[0-9]+$')
executed=$(/usr/bin/grep -cE '^(ok|not ok) ' out.tap)
[ "$declared" = "$executed" ] || echo "shortfall: $((declared - executed))"
```


## Detection tooling

For anyone who wants to check an existing suite, I published the two checks I used while
investigating this: https://github.com/KinohTaGo/bats-ghost-test-check

The static one (scan `@test` names for non-ASCII) is the one worth wiring into CI — the
dynamic declared-vs-executed check runs bats and therefore inherits the same locale
condition that triggers the bug, so it reports clean on a runner with `LC_ALL` unset.
